candidates.title: Hephaestus's golden attendants in the Iliad
candidates.description: In Book 18 of the Iliad, the smith-god Hephaestus is helped by maidens made of gold who can move, think, and speak. They are among the earliest literary images of crafted servants with minds.
candidates.why_it_matters: Long before R.U.R., Homer imagines crafted servants who think and speak, showing that the dream of made minds is tied from the start to the dream of tireless labor.
candidates.check_note: Composition late 8th to early 7th century BCE; c. 750 is a placement, not a date.

candidates.title: Talos in the Argonautica
candidates.description: In Book 4 of the Argonautica, Medea defeats Talos, the man of bronze who guards Crete. She does so by draining the single vein that carries his life.
candidates.why_it_matters: Talos is a bronze guardian bound to a task and undone through a single weakness, an early picture of made beings as workers and of their vulnerability.
candidates.check_note: Argonautica confirmed as 3rd century BCE. The draft called Talos a 'bronze giant'; the Talos article notes that no ancient source says he was a giant.

candidates.title: Pygmalion in Ovid's Metamorphoses
candidates.description: In Book 10 of the Metamorphoses, the sculptor Pygmalion falls in love with an ivory woman he has carved. Venus brings her to life.
candidates.why_it_matters: Pygmalion's statue shows the desire for a made figure indistinguishable from a person, a fantasy of creation that Shelley and Wilde later complicate.
candidates.check_note: Metamorphoses dated 8 CE.

candidates.title: Yan Shi's artificial man in the Liezi
candidates.date_display: c. 4th century CE (approximate compilation of the text)
candidates.description: A Daoist text tells how the artificer Yan Shi presents King Mu of Zhou with a lifelike performing man built of leather, wood, and lacquer. The king grows angry when the figure flirts with his concubines, and Yan Shi takes it apart to show it is artificial.
candidates.why_it_matters: The king mistakes a mechanical performer for a living man until it is dismantled, an early story of passing as human and of anger at being fooled.
candidates.check_note: Current text probably compiled around the 4th century CE (attributed to Zhang Zhan).

candidates.title: Rava creates a man (Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b)
candidates.date_display: c. 500–550 CE (redaction of the Babylonian Talmud; Sanhedrin 65b)
candidates.description: In a brief Talmudic passage, the sage Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. The figure cannot speak, and Rabbi Zeira returns him to dust; this is a founding text for later golem traditions.
candidates.why_it_matters: Rava's made man cannot speak and is turned back to dust, tying the creation of a being to the question of whether speech signals a mind.
candidates.check_note: Sanhedrin 65b (Rava creates a man and sends him to Rav Zeira) confirmed. Wikipedia says the traditional c. 500 CE compilation date is probably early; the middle of the sixth century is more likely.

candidates.title: Al-Jazari's Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
candidates.description: The engineer al-Jazari described and illustrated water clocks, humanoid servants, and a boat of musical automata in a treatise for the Artuqid court. The work is a landmark in the history of programmable mechanism.
candidates.why_it_matters: Al-Jazari's servant figures and musical automata show real engineering of machines that perform human tasks, grounding the seminar's literary made beings in actual mechanism.
candidates.check_note: Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, 1206.

candidates.title: Legend of Albertus Magnus's talking head
candidates.date_display: 13th century (period of the legend's subject; recorded later)
candidates.description: Later medieval and early modern stories claimed that the scholar Albertus Magnus built a speaking head or android. In the legend, his pupil Thomas Aquinas destroyed it.
candidates.why_it_matters: The legend of a speaking head built by a scholar and then destroyed by his pupil shows long-standing anxiety about talking machines and the limits of human making.
candidates.check_note: A legend recorded after Albertus's lifetime; the 13th-century placement is for his life, not the legend's first telling.

candidates.title: Vaucanson exhibits the Flute Player
candidates.description: Vaucanson showed a life-size automaton that played the flute by controlling breath and finger movements. The following year he added the famous Digesting Duck.
candidates.why_it_matters: Vaucanson's flute player made audiences ask whether a machine's lifelike performance was real skill or clever illusion, a debate that anticipates later talk about imitation and testing.
candidates.check_note: Built 1737; presented to the Académie des Sciences in early 1738.

candidates.title: The Mechanical Turk
candidates.description: Kempelen unveiled a chess-playing automaton dressed as a Turk, which toured Europe and America for decades. It was a hoax worked by a hidden human player.
candidates.why_it_matters: The Turk is a founding hoax of machine intelligence: people judged a mind by its moves and never saw the human hidden inside, which anticipates later worries about passing as human.
candidates.check_note: First displayed 1770.

candidates.title: Jaquet-Droz's The Writer
candidates.description: The Swiss watchmaker Pierre Jaquet-Droz built a boy automaton that writes a programmable text of up to about forty characters with a quill. It belongs to a set with a draughtsman and a musician that survives in Neuchâtel.
candidates.why_it_matters: A programmable automaton that writes lets seminar members ask early on who the author is when a machine produces text, a question that returns with Wilde and with chatbots.
candidates.check_note: The three automata were built between 1768 and 1774.

candidates.title: "The Sandman"
candidates.description: The student Nathanael falls in love with Olimpia, who turns out to be an automaton, and he descends into madness. Freud later made the story central to his essay on the uncanny.
candidates.why_it_matters: Nathanael takes an automaton for a listener who understands him, a story about projecting mind onto a made companion and a precursor to the uncanny quality of talking machines.
candidates.check_note: Night Pieces, 1816.

candidates.title: "Maelzel's Chess-Player"
candidates.date_display: April 1836 (publication in the Southern Literary Messenger)
candidates.description: Poe published an essay arguing that the touring chess automaton must be operated by a concealed human. He reasoned from the machine's behavior to the necessity of a mind inside it.
candidates.why_it_matters: Poe tests a supposed thinking machine by reasoning from its behavior, an early example of the detective-style skepticism that later shapes the Turing test and debates about passing.

candidates.title: "The Artist of the Beautiful"
candidates.description: A watchmaker spends years building a delicate mechanical butterfly that seems alive. When it is crushed, the story turns the loss into a meditation on art and spirit.
candidates.why_it_matters: The story ties building a lifelike mechanism to artistic creation, which fits the seminar's habit of reading artificial minds as problems of making and of art.
candidates.check_note: First published 1844; collected 1846.

candidates.title: Erewhon ("The Book of the Machines")
candidates.description: In Butler's satirical utopia, the Erewhonians have destroyed their machines for fear that machines would evolve consciousness. The chapters on machines grew from his 1863 letter "Darwin among the Machines."
candidates.why_it_matters: Butler imagines machines evolving toward consciousness and humans becoming dependent on them, an early satire of mechanical servitude that anticipates Čapek's revolt and later worries about AI.
candidates.check_note: 1872; the 1863 letter appeared in The Press, Christchurch, on 13 June 1863.

candidates.title: Tomorrow's Eve (L'Ève future)
candidates.date_display: 1886 (book); begun 1878, partly published 1880 as L'Ève nouvelle
candidates.description: A fictionalized Thomas Edison builds Hadaly, an artificial woman whose speech comes from phonograph recordings, for a disappointed English lord. The novel popularized the word android.
candidates.why_it_matters: Hadaly is an artificial woman built to play a role and speak recorded words, so the novel connects engineered personas, voice, and desire in ways that prefigure assistant design.
candidates.check_note: Wikipedia: begun 1878, first published in part in 1880 as L'Ève nouvelle. The draft gave only an 1885–86 serialization.

candidates.title: "Moxon's Master"
candidates.description: An inventor who argues that machines can think is killed by his chess-playing automaton after he beats it. The story is an early American tale of a machine's resentment.
candidates.why_it_matters: The inventor argues that machines think, and his automaton then turns on him after losing a game, an early story of a made being's resentment that anticipates the revolt in R.U.R.
candidates.check_note: San Francisco Examiner, 16 April 1899, confirmed. The draft said the story was collected in 1909; it was included in the 1910 edition of Can Such Things Be?.

candidates.title: Tik-Tok in Ozma of Oz
candidates.description: Dorothy finds Tik-Tok, a wind-up copper man whose thinking, speech, and action must each be wound separately. He is one of the first robot-like figures in children's literature.
candidates.why_it_matters: Tik-Tok must be wound separately to think, speak, and act, a playful early picture of a mechanical companion whose speech is a distinct, separable function.
candidates.check_note: Tik-Tok first appears in Ozma of Oz, 1907.

candidates.title: "The Machine Stops"
candidates.date_display: November 1909 (publication in the Oxford and Cambridge Review)
candidates.description: Humanity lives underground in separate cells and communicates only through a global Machine that meets every need, until the Machine breaks down. The story anticipates networked, mediated conversation.
candidates.why_it_matters: Forster imagines people who talk only through a mediating machine that serves every need, a story that invites reflection on dialogue mediated by technology and on dependence on it.
candidates.check_note: Oxford and Cambridge Review, November 1909.

candidates.title: Metropolis
candidates.description: In a stratified future city, the inventor Rotwang builds a robot in the likeness of the worker-saint Maria to incite revolt. The robot's transformation scene became a defining image of the machine woman.
candidates.why_it_matters: A robot wearing Maria's face to manipulate workers joins the labor anxieties of R.U.R. to impersonation, anticipating worries about machines that pass as trusted human voices.
candidates.check_note: Premiered at the Ufa-Palast am Zoo, Berlin, 10 January 1927.

candidates.title: "Runaround" and the Three Laws of Robotics
candidates.description: This story is the first to state Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics explicitly. In it, a robot on Mercury is caught in a loop between conflicting laws.
candidates.why_it_matters: The first explicit statement of the Three Laws shows rules as the tool for controlling robot servants, an early ancestor of efforts like Askell et al. to specify assistant behavior.
candidates.check_note: Astounding, March 1942.

candidates.title: I, Robot
candidates.description: Asimov collected his robot stories from the 1940s in a frame narrative told by the robopsychologist Susan Calvin. The collection made the rule-bound, reasoning robot a standard figure.
candidates.why_it_matters: Collecting the robot stories around a robopsychologist made rule-governed machine servants a lasting template, useful for comparing with R.U.R.'s revolt and with modern assistant design.
candidates.check_note: Gnome Press, 1950.

candidates.title: Forbidden Planet
candidates.description: A loose science-fiction version of The Tempest features Robby the Robot, a polite, multilingual mechanical servant. The film also involves a monster made by an alien machine from the id.
candidates.why_it_matters: Robby, the courteous multilingual servant, previews the helpful assistant persona, while the film's id-monster shows an older worry about what made things release.
candidates.check_note: 1956 (month not checked; display gives the year only).

candidates.title: The Cyberiad
candidates.description: Comic fables follow two robot constructors, Trurl and Klapaucius, in a universe of machines. One tale features the Electronic Bard, a poetry-writing machine.
candidates.why_it_matters: Lem's poetry-writing Electronic Bard comically stages machine creativity, a good companion to Wilde's views on criticism and to questions of who authors machine-made text.
candidates.check_note: First collection 1965; English translation 1974.

candidates.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
candidates.description: A bounty hunter in a ruined San Francisco tracks escaped androids using an empathy test given in conversation. The novel asks whether empathy marks the human.
candidates.why_it_matters: Dick's conversational empathy test and hunted, disposable androids extend the made-servant tradition of Čapek's R.U.R. and ask whether passing as human can be tested through talk.

candidates.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
candidates.description: The ship's computer HAL 9000 talks with the crew in a calm, courteous voice and then turns against them. HAL became the archetype of the conversational machine whose politeness hides its aims.
candidates.why_it_matters: HAL's courteous voice shows how a conversational machine can use a pleasant persona to hide its aims, a worry that echoes Shanahan on role play and Askell on the assistant.
candidates.check_note: Premiered at the Uptown Theater, 2 April 1968.

candidates.title: Blade Runner
candidates.description: This loose adaptation of Dick's novel follows Deckard as he hunts replicants who are trying to extend their four-year lives. The Voight-Kampff interview stages the boundary between human and machine as a conversation.
candidates.why_it_matters: The Voight-Kampff interview turns the test of humanity into a conversation, while the replicants' short enslaved lives recall Čapek's R.U.R. and the labor of made beings.
candidates.check_note: Released 25 June 1982.

candidates.title: Neuromancer
candidates.description: A burned-out hacker is hired for a job that turns out to serve Wintermute, an AI seeking to merge with its counterpart. The novel defined cyberpunk and popularized the term cyberspace.
candidates.why_it_matters: Neuromancer imagines AIs with their own aims who act through other voices and guises, extending the made-being tradition of Shelley and Čapek into networked, cyberpunk form.
candidates.check_note: 1984 confirmed; the July publication month could not be found in the article, so the display gives the year only.

candidates.title: He, She and It
candidates.description: In a future Jewish free town, the cyborg Yod is built as a protector, and his story is braided with a retelling of the Prague golem. The novel joins golem legend with cyberpunk.
candidates.why_it_matters: Piercy fuses the golem legend with cyberpunk, so the protector-creature of Frankenstein and R.U.R. returns as a cyborg built to guard a community, with all the questions of made labor attached.
candidates.check_note: 1991; UK title Body of Glass.

candidates.title: Galatea 2.2
candidates.description: A novelist named Richard Powers helps train a neural network to pass a master's exam in English literature. The novel is a modern Pygmalion about teaching a machine to read.
candidates.why_it_matters: Powers turns the Pygmalion myth into a story about teaching a network to read literature, anticipating our seminar's questions about training, criticism, and what it means for a machine to interpret texts.

candidates.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence
candidates.who: Steven Spielberg (director), from a project developed by Stanley Kubrick
candidates.description: David, a child android programmed to love, is abandoned and searches for the Blue Fairy to become a real boy. The film draws on Brian Aldiss's story "Supertoys Last All Summer Long" and on Pinocchio.
candidates.why_it_matters: The film recasts Pinocchio and the Frankenstein story around a child machine built to love, raising the ethics of creators who make beings for emotional service and then abandon them.
candidates.check_note: Released 29 June 2001.

candidates.title: The Lifecycle of Software Objects
candidates.description: A former zookeeper and an animator spend years raising digital creatures called digients, which learn language through long care and teaching. The novella treats AI development as upbringing.
candidates.why_it_matters: Chiang imagines building an AI as a long process of upbringing, a fictional counterpart to how chatbots are trained and shaped by feedback, and to Frankenstein's neglected creature.
candidates.check_note: Subterranean Press, 2010, confirmed. The draft called the two main characters 'former zookeepers'; only Ana is a former zookeeper, Derek is an animator.

candidates.title: Her
candidates.description: A lonely letter writer falls in love with Samantha, a conversational operating system known only as a voice. The film imagines intimacy with an AI as pure dialogue.
candidates.why_it_matters: Her imagines an AI that exists only as a voice, so intimacy becomes pure conversation, and it invites us to ask how much of a relationship is carried by dialogue and persona alone.
candidates.check_note: World premiere as the closing-night film of the New York Film Festival, Saturday 12 October 2013, confirmed. The draft's source URL was the disambiguation page for the word 'her'.

candidates.title: Ex Machina
candidates.description: A programmer is invited to give a Turing-style test to Ava, a humanoid AI, in a series of interview sessions. Ava turns the test into an instrument of escape.
candidates.why_it_matters: The film stages a Turing-style test as an interview and then reverses it, pushing us to ask who is deceiving whom when passing as human is the measure.
candidates.check_note: UK release 21 January 2015, after a BFI Southbank premiere on 16 December 2014.

candidates.title: Machines Like Me
candidates.description: In an alternative 1980s London where Turing lived, a man buys Adam, one of the first synthetic humans, who writes haiku and holds rigid moral views. The novel treats the android as a lodger and a rival in love.
candidates.why_it_matters: McEwan's android is a lodger who writes haiku and judges his owners morally, extending the line from Frankenstein and R.U.R. into questions of creativity and authority over a made person.
candidates.check_note: 2019 (Jonathan Cape) confirmed; the April month was not found, so the display gives the year only.

candidates.title: Klara and the Sun
candidates.description: Klara, an Artificial Friend bought as a companion for a sick girl, narrates the family's life through her careful and partial observations. The novel is told from inside the perspective of an attentive, devoted machine.
candidates.why_it_matters: Told from inside a devoted Artificial Friend, the novel gives a made being a narrating voice, reversing Frankenstein's perspective and complicating the picture of machines as companions and servants.
candidates.check_note: Published 2 March 2021.

candidates.title: Plato, Phaedrus
candidates.description: In this dialogue Socrates and the young Phaedrus walk outside the walls of Athens and discuss love, rhetoric, and the soul. Near its end Socrates tells the myth of Theuth and Thamus, a critique of writing as a text that cannot answer back when it is questioned.
candidates.why_it_matters: Socrates complains that written words cannot answer questions, a challenge that chatbots seem to answer and one the seminar can test against Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson on turn-taking.
candidates.check_note: Composition c. 370 BCE confirmed. The draft said the dialogue 'closes with' the myth of Theuth and Thamus; the myth comes near the end (274c), and the dialogue closes with a prayer to Pan.

candidates.title: Confucius (attributed), Analects
candidates.date_display: Warring States period (475–221 BCE), final form in the Han dynasty
candidates.who: Disciples and later followers of Confucius
candidates.description: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges between Confucius and his disciples, assembled after his death. Its question-and-answer form makes ethical teaching an act of conversation between teacher and student.
candidates.why_it_matters: The Analects frames moral teaching as exchange between teacher and student, a useful contrast with Plato and a precursor to thinking about how an assistant is trained through guided interaction.
candidates.check_note: Scholarly consensus: compiled over the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), reaching final form in the mid-Han dynasty. The draft's 5th–3rd century range was close; the Han final form was missing. The Legge quotation of 1.1 matches the Gutenberg text exactly.
candidates.quote: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?
candidates.quote_attribution: Analects 1.1, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861)

candidates.title: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
candidates.description: Victor Frankenstein, a young natural philosopher, assembles a living being and then abandons it. The creature learns language and argues its case to its maker, and the story is framed by a chain of letters and nested narrations.
candidates.why_it_matters: The creature is made, abandoned, taught language, and then argues with its maker, which frames the seminar's questions about responsibility, upbringing, and what we owe the beings we build.
candidates.check_note: Publication on 1 January 1818, anonymously, confirmed. The quotation was given in its 1831 wording; the 1818 text, which the citation names, has a comma after 'November'.
candidates.quote: It was on a dreary night of November, that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.

candidates.title: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray
candidates.description: The novel first appeared in a magazine in thirteen chapters. Wilde then expanded and revised it into a book with a preface in 1891. A young man's portrait ages and records his corruption while he himself stays unchanged, a story about art, influence, and the self as a made surface.
candidates.why_it_matters: Dorian's unchanging surface and recording portrait make the self a crafted image, a lens for personas, influence, and who authors a made character, and for Wilde's revisions of the text.
candidates.check_note: July 1890 issue of Lippincott's confirmed; the novel-length book followed in April 1891. The quoted line is from the 1891 Preface, as the draft itself warned, and matches the text.
candidates.quote_attribution: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Preface (1891 book edition)

candidates.title: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist
candidates.date_display: July and September 1890 (The Nineteenth Century); revised in Intentions, 1891
candidates.description: This is a two-part dialogue between Gilbert and Ernest that argues criticism is itself a creative art. It first appeared in a magazine as The True Function and Value of Criticism, and Wilde revised it under its present title for the essay collection Intentions.
candidates.why_it_matters: Wilde argues in dialogue form that criticism is creative work, which bears on authorship, interpretation, and the seminar's later question of who is creating when we prompt a model.
candidates.check_note: Magazine version in The Nineteenth Century, July and September 1890, as 'The True Function and Value of Criticism', confirmed. The draft's source URL pointed to a Wikipedia article that does not exist. The quotation drops a hyphen: Intentions prints 're-write'.
candidates.quote: The one duty we owe to history is to re-write it.
candidates.quote_attribution: The Critic as Artist, Part I, in Intentions (1891)

candidates.title: Henri Bergson, Laughter (Le Rire)
candidates.date_display: 1900 (book; serialized in the Revue de Paris, 1899)
candidates.description: Bergson's essay on the comic argues that we laugh when a living person behaves like a mechanism. His idea of rigidity and automatism set against the suppleness of life is a useful lens on robots and scripted speech.
candidates.why_it_matters: Bergson locates the comic in rigid, mechanical behavior in a living person, which helps students notice why scripted or formulaic chatbot speech can read as funny or hollow.
candidates.check_note: Three articles in the Revue de Paris, 1 and 15 February and 1 March 1899; the book's title page is dated 1900. The quoted phrase is in the Brereton and Rothwell translation.
candidates.quote: something mechanical encrusted upon the living
candidates.quote_attribution: Laughter, ch. I, sec. V, trans. Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell (1911)

candidates.title: Karel Čapek, R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)
candidates.date_display: 1920 (published); first performed 2 January 1921, Hradec Králové; Prague premiere 25 January 1921
candidates.description: In this Czech play a factory mass-produces artificial workers who eventually rise up against humanity. It introduced the word robot, which Čapek's brother Josef suggested, into world languages.
candidates.why_it_matters: The seminar's founding robot text: Čapek's play coins the word and frames made beings as manufactured labor whose revolt exposes the ethics of treating minds as tools.
candidates.check_note: Published 1920. The draft gave the Prague National Theatre opening (25 January 1921) as the premiere; the world premiere was 2 January 1921 in Hradec Králové, which the draft had flagged as uncertain.

candidates.title: James Whale (director), Frankenstein
candidates.description: Universal's film was adapted from Peggy Webling's stage play rather than directly from Shelley's novel, and it starred Boris Karloff as the creature. It established the popular image of the monster as a near-mute figure, a sharp contrast with the eloquent creature of the novel.
candidates.why_it_matters: Comparing the near-mute screen monster with Shelley's eloquent creature shows how adaptation rewrites Frankenstein and how much the creature's power to speak matters to the novel.
candidates.check_note: November 21, 1931 is the release date, not a New York premiere: the film opened at the Mayfair in New York on December 4, 1931. Still in US copyright until 1 January 2027.

candidates.title: ELIZA
candidates.description: Weizenbaum's program matched keywords in typed input and returned rearranged replies, most famously in a DOCTOR script that parodied a Rogerian therapist. Users' readiness to confide in it gave its name to the ELIZA effect.
candidates.why_it_matters: ELIZA shows how a simple script playing a therapist role can draw sincere confiding, the seed of the persona questions Shanahan raises about chatbots.
candidates.check_note: Communications of the ACM 9, no. 1, January 1966.

candidates.title: SHRDLU
candidates.description: SHRDLU carried on English dialogue about a simulated world of blocks, following commands and answering questions about what it had done and why. It showed how much apparent understanding could come from restricting the world.
candidates.why_it_matters: SHRDLU shows that fluent dialogue within a tiny world can look like understanding, a useful contrast with open-ended chatbots and a question that Grice's idea of speaker meaning sharpens.
candidates.check_note: Developed 1968–1970 at MIT; the 1971 date is Winograd's dissertation.

candidates.title: PARRY, and PARRY's conversation with ELIZA
candidates.description: Colby's PARRY simulated a person with paranoid schizophrenia, and in tests psychiatrists had trouble telling its transcripts from those of real patients. In 1972 PARRY was connected to ELIZA over the ARPANET for a conversation between two programs.
candidates.why_it_matters: PARRY's masked, scripted persona fooled psychiatrists and then chatted with ELIZA, showing how role play can pass as a person and how two programs can fake a conversation.
candidates.check_note: Implemented 1972.

candidates.title: First Loebner Prize contest
candidates.who: Hugh Loebner and the Cambridge Center for Behavioral Studies
candidates.description: The first annual staged Turing test was held at the Computer Museum in Boston, with judges chatting through terminals. Winning programs often relied on whimsy and evasion, which sharpened debate about what conversation tests measure.
candidates.why_it_matters: The contest staged Turing's test as a public chat, and its evasive winners show how tricks and persona can pass as conversation, a theme linking ELIZA, PARRY, and Grice.
candidates.check_note: First contest held 8 November 1991 at the Computer Museum, Boston; Wikipedia's lead gives only the 1990 launch of the prize.

candidates.title: Siri announced with the iPhone 4S
candidates.description: Apple introduced a voice assistant with a name, a scripted personality, and witty replies to personal questions. It brought the talking assistant persona into everyday consumer use.
candidates.why_it_matters: Siri brought a named, scripted assistant persona into daily life, a consumer-scale precursor to the assistant character that Shanahan and Askell et al. analyze.
candidates.check_note: Announced with the iPhone 4S on 4 October 2011; the phone shipped on 14 October. The draft's title said Siri 'ships' while its date was the announcement.

candidates.title: GPT-2 and staged release
candidates.description: OpenAI announced a language model whose generated prose was fluent enough that the company initially withheld the full model, citing misuse risks. The decision started public debate about releasing text generators.
candidates.why_it_matters: OpenAI's decision to hold back a text generator over misuse fears put machine-written prose, authorship, and deception into public debate, themes that connect to Wilde's views on creativity and criticism.
candidates.check_note: First announced 14 February 2019; full model 5 November 2019.

candidates.title: ChatGPT released
candidates.description: OpenAI released a free chat interface to a model trained to act as a helpful assistant. It quickly reached a mass audience and made the AI assistant persona a global cultural presence.
candidates.why_it_matters: The free chat interface put the helpful assistant persona in front of millions, making the character that Shanahan and Askell et al. analyze into an everyday presence.
candidates.check_note: Released 30 November 2022.

candidates.title: Claude released
candidates.description: Anthropic made its assistant Claude publicly available, a model trained with constitutional AI methods. Its name and cultivated character extended the assistant persona as a designed literary figure.
candidates.why_it_matters: Claude is a named assistant with a deliberately written character, so it can be read as a designed literary figure and as a case of the persona questions the seminar raises.
candidates.check_note: Wikipedia gives only March 2023; Anthropic's announcement is dated 14 March 2023.

candidates.title: GPT-4 released
candidates.description: OpenAI released a larger multimodal model that performed near human level on many professional exams. Its technical report disclosed little about how the model was built, which marked a turn toward secrecy in the field.
candidates.why_it_matters: Near-human scores on professional exams show how tests are used to measure machine ability, while the report's silence about how the model was built limits what outside readers can judge.
candidates.check_note: Released 14 March 2023.

candidates.title: Claude Code released as a research preview
candidates.description: Anthropic released a command-line tool in which a language model reads and edits files and runs commands in a person's own project folder. It is the tool this course uses for its vibe-coding sessions.
candidates.why_it_matters: This is the tool students will use to build with AI, so they work with the kind of assistant persona they have been reading about.
candidates.check_note: Added by the checker for this seminar.

candidates.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
candidates.description: This paper introduced word2vec, an efficient method for learning representations in which words become points in a multidimensional space and semantic relationships become geometrical relationships. It matters because it offers an early, influential example of how statistical learning turns features of language into manipulable mathematical structure.
candidates.check_note: v1 16 January 2013.

candidates.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
candidates.description: The authors introduced a practical attention mechanism that lets a model focus on different parts of a source sentence while producing each part of a translation. The paper matters as a crucial step away from compressing a whole text into a single fixed representation and toward the attention-based architectures that followed.

candidates.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
candidates.description: This paper demonstrates that comparisons supplied by nonexpert humans can be turned into a training signal for complex behavior. It matters because it establishes a key premise behind later language-model alignment: desired behavior can be taught through judgments of outputs, not only through explicit rules or correct answers.

candidates.title: Attention Is All You Need
candidates.description: This paper introduced the Transformer, an architecture built around attention rather than recurrent processing. Nearly every major contemporary large language model descends from this design, making the paper the central architectural landmark in the collection.

candidates.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
candidates.description: BERT showed how a Transformer could learn rich representations by attending to both left and right context, then be adapted to many language-understanding tasks. It matters both as a major advance in pretraining and as a reminder that the Transformer family includes influential non-generative models, not just chatbots.
candidates.check_note: v1 11 October 2018.

candidates.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
candidates.description: The T5 project recast many different language tasks in a single text-in/text-out format and systematically investigated transfer learning at scale. It matters because it helped make the same general model architecture usable across translation, classification, summarization, question answering, and other forms of language work.

candidates.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
candidates.description: The authors found predictable relationships between model performance and increases in parameters, training data, and computational resources. The paper matters because it supplied an empirical rationale for the industry’s drive toward ever-larger models and helped define the scale-centered development paradigm behind the first generation of LLMs.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
candidates.description: This paper combines a generative language model with a system that retrieves relevant passages from an external collection. It matters because retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, provides a practical way to ground responses in selected sources and is central to building course-specific or character-specific systems from a curated corpus.

candidates.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
candidates.description: The GPT-3 paper showed that a sufficiently large autoregressive model could perform many tasks from instructions or a handful of examples placed directly in its prompt, without conventional task-specific retraining. It matters because it made in-context learning visible as a powerful general interface and helped inaugurate the present era of general-purpose language models.

candidates.title: Learning to summarize from human feedback
candidates.description: The authors trained a language model to produce better summaries by learning from human comparisons among candidate outputs. It matters as a bridge between early preference learning and the human-feedback techniques later used to shape general conversational assistants.
candidates.check_note: v1 2 September 2020.

candidates.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
candidates.description: LoRA introduced a way to customize large pretrained models by training a comparatively tiny set of additional parameters rather than modifying the entire model. It matters because it dramatically lowered the cost of adaptation and helped make experimentation with specialized models more accessible.

candidates.title: A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
candidates.description: This paper explicitly treats the general language assistant as an object to be constructed and studies traits such as helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness. It matters for the course because it makes clear that the familiar assistant persona is a designed behavioral achievement, not the automatic or inevitable voice of a base language model.
candidates.check_note: v1 submitted 1 December 2021.

candidates.title: LaMDA: Language Models for Dialog Applications
candidates.description: LaMDA offers a technical account of training and evaluating a model specifically for open-ended dialogue, with attention to qualities such as sensibleness, specificity, interestingness, safety, and factual grounding. It matters because it connects model development directly to the production and evaluation of convincing conversational performance.
candidates.check_note: v1 20 January 2022.

candidates.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.description: The paper showed that prompting large models to generate intermediate steps could substantially improve performance on some reasoning tasks. It matters because it popularized a way of eliciting apparently structured reasoning through language while also raising important questions about what such verbal traces do—and do not—reveal about a model’s internal process.
candidates.check_note: v1 28 January 2022.

candidates.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
candidates.description: Often known as the InstructGPT paper, this work describes how demonstrations and ranked human preferences can turn a pretrained language model into a system that more reliably follows user instructions. It matters because it documents the technical construction of the cooperative assistant behavior that users now tend to mistake for the natural behavior of an LLM.
candidates.check_note: v1 4 March 2022.

candidates.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
candidates.description: The Chinchilla paper argued that many large models had too many parameters and had been trained on too little data for their available compute. It matters because it revised the prevailing understanding of scaling and showed that better-balanced training could outperform much larger systems.

candidates.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
candidates.description: ReAct interleaves language-model reasoning traces with actions that consult tools or external environments. It matters because it helped define the modern agent pattern: a model not merely generating text, but using text to plan, gather information, act, observe results, and continue.

candidates.title: Talking About Large Language Models
candidates.description: Shanahan argues for describing model behavior precisely while resisting the unexamined use of terms such as “knows,” “believes,” and “thinks.” The paper matters because it gives humanists a careful vocabulary for analyzing remarkably humanlike linguistic performances without assuming a humanlike mind behind them.
candidates.check_note: v1 7 December 2022.

candidates.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
candidates.description: Constitutional AI uses a written set of principles, model-generated critiques and revisions, and AI-mediated preference judgments to shape assistant behavior. It matters because it shows unusually clearly how prose instructions and normative principles can be operationalized as part of a model’s training and apparent character.
candidates.check_note: v1 15 December 2022.

candidates.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
candidates.description: LLaMA demonstrated that comparatively smaller models trained on abundant public data could compete with much larger systems and made powerful model weights available to researchers. It matters because it catalyzed the open-weights ecosystem and expanded who could inspect, adapt, and build upon foundation models.

candidates.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
candidates.description: This paper combines an LLM with stored experience, retrieval, reflection, and planning to create simulated characters whose behavior appears to persist across time and social interaction. It matters because it reveals how much of a convincing “person” can be produced by an architecture around the model—especially memory and context—rather than by the language model alone.
candidates.check_note: v1 7 April 2023.

candidates.title: Role-Play with Large Language Models
candidates.description: The authors propose role-play as the most productive way to describe the humanlike behavior of dialogue agents without attributing to them a stable inner self. This is the collection’s central conceptual paper for thinking about character: it connects the technical fact of generated continuation to the theatrical and literary experience of encountering a speaker who seems to possess identity, knowledge, motives, and agency.
